key_insight: The paper shows that zero-temperature bias in amplitude damping mostly changes the scale of learned features, while the Pauli-twirled infinite-temperature version isolates the contraction effect and reveals when damping is effectively a gauge choice.
engineering_relevance: For noisy variational quantum circuits, a simple output rescaling can recover much of the accuracy lost to damping, but the same correction shifts the burden to measurement-shot cost and circuit-design choices.
method: Compare amplitude damping (AD) with its Pauli-twirled generalized amplitude damping counterpart across variational circuits.
Analyze feature scaling, damping-induced floors, and depth dependence under random parameters and trained output scaling.
Study how noise placement and circuit structure make damping either a removable gauge or a physical effect.
evidence_signal: Simulations up to eight qubits show AD features saturate to a damping-dependent floor, and with 10^3 shots per image a four-qubit classifier at p=0.3 stays within 1.5 percentage points of noiseless accuracy, while twirled versions can lose up to 33 points.
watch_item: The gauge interpretation depends on the noise occurring after complete entangling layers with trainable boundaries; inside decomposed two-qubit gates, the damping direction becomes physically meaningful.
paper_title: Zero- Versus Infinite-Temperature Damping in Variational Quantum Circuits: Feature Scale, Sampling Cost, and Frame Gauge
